title: A pricing page for a restaurant group
metaTitle: What a restaurant group pricing page shows
excerpt: Show the shape of dinner: what a night costs, what is included, and how to open the menu or book. Guests use that page to judge fit, not to do homework.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a quiet interior a guest might compare with the price of a night out.
caption: A room with a clear threshold. The price of dinner needs a threshold too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Do restaurants need a page called Pricing?
faqs.answer: They need a place where the shape of the spend is obvious. That can be the menu itself, with prices, plus a short note on service, wine, and private dining. A separate page helps when a PDF menu hides the numbers or when a tasting menu and a casual room would be confused. Call it whatever the guest would look for.

faqs.question: What should we publish if prices change weekly?
faqs.answer: Publish the model, and the current number where you have one. A set tasting price can be updated the day it changes. A la carte can say that dishes are priced on the menu and that a main sits in the band you already quote by phone. Hiding every figure because one special moves is how guests assume the worst.

faqs.question: How should private dining prices differ?
faqs.answer: Give them their own shape: minimum spend or a per-person menu, what is included, how many people, and how far ahead to ask. Do not bury a buyout minimum in the same line as a weeknight table for two. Link each shape to the right next step, menu or booking or a short inquiry.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A restaurant group pricing page is how a guest deciding where to go tonight judges fit. They are not building a spreadsheet. They want the shape of the night: what is included, what is not, and how to see the menu or book a table.

Show that shape if they will ask the host anyway. A menu that says "seasonal" and never says a number sends careful guests to the place that will speak plainly. The room got their appetite. The price tells them whether this is their night.

## Fit, in the guest's terms

This is not a software pricing table with three tiers and a toggle. Dinner does not come in Starter, Growth, and Enterprise. It comes as a counter, a dining room, a set menu, or a lunch that is a different product from Saturday. The page should use those words.

Say the model in the first screen, per restaurant if the group is mixed. "Dinner is a la carte. Mains are listed with prices on the menu." Or "Dinner is a set menu. The current price is on this page, and wine pairing is separate." Or "Lunch is a shorter menu at a lower spend than dinner." Pick the sentences that are true this week.

Nielsen Norman Group's note on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) matters because guests read only a fraction of the words. The shape has to be a heading and a few lines, not an essay about hospitality. If they cannot see whether this is a splurge before they scroll, they will leave to a place that shows the number.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone leaves knowing enough to act. Acting here means opening the real menu or booking the right room. If they still have to message you to learn whether a service charge is included, the page stopped early.

## The shape of a night

Write the shape a local already half-knows, and make it explicit.

- Which meal: lunch, dinner, or a weekend set.
- Whether the menu is a la carte or a set number of courses.
- The current set price, if there is one, and what that price buys.
- Where a la carte prices live, one tap away, as text.
- A plain line on wine: list prices on the list, pairing optional, corkage only if you allow it.
- Service: included, discretionary, or neither. Use the words your bill uses.

Do not invent a band to look transparent. Publish the band or the number you already say when a friend asks. If you will not say it on the phone, do not print a fantasy. If you say it on the phone every Friday, it belongs here.

Update the set price the day it changes. A wrong number is worse than a short delay while you edit. Make the figure a field the manager can change, not a number drawn inside a picture. On a Hanabi build the words that change should be editable. A price baked into a poster will lie by next season.

If two restaurants in the group sit at different spends, do not average them. Averaging is how a guest books the expensive room expecting the casual one. Give each room its own short block. Same headings. Different facts.

## What is included

Say what the price covers so the bill matches the promise. For a set menu: the courses, whether coffee is in, whether a snack at the bar is in. For a la carte: that each dish is priced on the menu, and whether bread or a cover charge appears.

Say the service charge in the same sentence family as the food price. Guests feel tricked when a percentage appears only on the slip. If it is discretionary, say that. If it is included, say that, and do not also invite a tip in a way that double-counts unless you mean to. The page should match the bill.

Pairing is its own included-or-not line. "Pairing is optional and priced per person on the menu" is a shape. "We have a beautiful wine program" is not. Guests who do not drink need to see that the food price stands alone. Guests who do drink need to see that the pairing is not a surprise second menu.

Tax and card fees, if they surprise people in your city, get one clause. You do not need a legal memorandum. You need the sentence the host is tired of repeating.

## What is not included

Exclusions are how you protect the floor and the guest.

Wine and cocktails, unless a package says otherwise. Corkage, and whether you allow it. Cake from outside, and any plate charge. Private room hire if it is separate from the minimum spend. A special menu for a holiday that replaces the ordinary one. Valet or a cloak if you charge.

List them where they can be scanned. A pale footer is where trust goes to hide. A guest planning a birthday will read the cake line if it has a heading. They will not read it inside a paragraph about the garden.

Private dining should not be an exclusion stuffed under dinner. It is a different product. Give it a block: how many people, the minimum or the per-person menu, what the room includes, and how to ask. The next step may be a short note rather than the public booking widget. Say which. A widget that cannot hold a buyout will create a false confirmation.

If a restaurant in the group is counter-only and another takes bookings, the price page must say that too. A set price for a room you cannot reserve is a different night from a walk-in bowl. Fit includes the way you get the seat, not only the bill.

## From the number to the menu or the table

Put the actions next to the shape they belong to. Under the casual room: Menu, Book a table. Under the set menu: the price, then Book, with the party size the book can actually take. Under private dining: the minimum, then a short inquiry that asks for date, headcount, and meal.

Do not use one generic Reserve for all three. The guest will land in the wrong flow and the floor will unwind it by phone. The page exists to prevent that phone call, or to make it a better one.

Keep the form for private dining short. Date, number of people, which room, a contact. Ten fields, including how they heard of you, will lose the table. The public booking link should already know the venue.

Tell them what the booking confirmation means. A held table. A deposit, if there is one, and whether it comes off the bill. The deposit amount is part of the price shape. Hiding it until the last click is how guests abandon a booking they would have accepted if they had known.

If the shapes are still muddy and you want them settled before the page is designed, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current menus and the sentence your hosts already use about what dinner costs. The call should separate weeknight tables from buyouts, and decide which numbers are public. Hanabi designs and builds the site after that. The prices stay yours to change.

## A page you can correct on a Thursday

Prices move. The page has to move the same day, by someone who is not waiting on a designer. Treat each restaurant's block as content: model, number or link, inclusions, exclusions, button. A beautiful static image of a menu is how Thursday's change waits until next month.

Test the page on a phone, because the guest is comparing you in a group chat. The set price should be visible without pinch-zoom. The menu link should open. The book button should carry the right venue. Read the inclusions against last night's bill. If they disagree, fix the page before service, not after a review.

The limit of the page is that it cannot quote a custom menu for a wedding. It can stop the wrong-fit booking and start the right one. That is enough. Do not turn it into a catering catalog unless catering is truly a product you want this week.

Walk the page against three guests before you publish it. A pair booking a weeknight. A family comparing lunch. A host arranging a private room. Each should find their number, their inclusion, and their button without reading the other two blocks. If the family lands on the tasting price and panics, the headings are too soft. If the host cannot see the minimum, the buyout is still a rumor. Fix those three paths. They are the whole page. A fourth audience, the person writing a review of your brand, can wait. Tonight's guest will not.

## The offers, in guest language

A price still floats if the guest cannot see what they are buying besides food. Dinner, a private room, lunch, a group table. Those are the offers. Each needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. A grid that says "experiences" will not do it.

Read [the services page a restaurant group actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-restaurant-group-actually-needs) before you add another price block. Name the nights you actually sell. Then let the price page sit beside those names, not instead of them.
